questions.explain: The chapter notes Standard Edition is limited to 24 cores and 128 GB per instance, and a 32-core Enterprise instance costs several times its Standard equivalent.
questions.q: SQL Server Standard Edition is limited to how many cores per instance — a limit worth checking before paying for Enterprise?

questions.explain: Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you bring existing licenses with Software Assurance to Azure SQL, cutting compute costs roughly in half versus license-included pricing.
questions.q: Which licensing program lets you bring existing SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance to Azure and cut compute costs roughly in half?

questions.explain: An index that is never read (zero seeks/scans/lookups) is pure overhead — it consumes storage and adds write overhead on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.
options: They are required by the optimizer
They consume storage and add write overhead on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
questions.q: Why are unused indexes a cost problem, not just a storage problem?

questions.explain: The chapter says to prioritize queries by total resource consumption: a 200ms query firing 50,000 times per hour is the real cost driver, not a 5-second query run weekly.
options: The query with the longest single execution time
The query with the highest total resource consumption (e.g., top total_worker_time in sys.dm_exec_query_stats)
The query with the most JOINs
questions.q: Which queries should you optimize first to reduce infrastructure cost?

questions.explain: Reserved instances offer 30–60% discounts for one- or three-year commitments, and there is almost no argument against reserving a production database that will run for the next year.
options: Reserved instances for one- or three-year commitments
questions.q: For a stable production database that will definitely run for the next year, which pricing option typically saves 30–60% over on-demand?
